commentBody: Sam writes: The New York Times Crossword defines a rebus as a theme element that requires the solver to enter more than one letter into a square. Sam, Too limited IMO. It's not just squishes. "Some puzzles require you to use symbols or to cram more than one letter into a single box." https://www.xwordinfo.com/Rebus

We’ve seen similar themes like this before, but usually with corny word puns (confession: my first published puzzle with the WSJ was one) but never in John Kugelman’s inimicable style and with such eye catching visual diversions. I was completely charmed and delighted, not only by the theme but by the rest of John’s signature clues and entries. My favorite by far was NUN, but gotta love STOP sign of the cross KOOSH and INCOGMEATO and YESANDS as a verb and PEACHEMOJI and FURSONAS…I expect a hecka (make that HELLA) lot of comments today that I can’t wait to read. One misdirection a YAK has thick skin too no? Anyways, a Kugelman that didn’t disappoint, me at least. Here’s another Crosshare share from me, my one and only themeless attempt. I don’t fault that it wasn’t published, I don’t think it was quite there, but I did love the spanners and the first two downs, so have at it and tell me what you think: https://crosshare.org/crosswords/CC2SHU4Y2Hmc3YOlFclk/where-its-at-themeless

So, not only did John have to come up with mashup movie titles, but he had to find those for which clue pictures could be made.  After all, what kind of picture could be made with, say, SINGIN’ IN THE RAIN MAN?

That made coming up with theme answers one layer more difficult.  Add to that, he had to come up with three pairs of theme answers, each with the same number of letters to fit symmetry.

Bravo on that!

I loved learning that there is no single word for “please” in the Danish language.  But don’t think Danes are impolite.  Post solve, I learned there are Danish phrases with that meaning, such as one that translates to “…be so kind as to”.

And man, it was fun trying to guess the theme answers with as few crosses as possible just from the pictures.

John, this is your ninth puzzle so far this year, four of them Sundays, and all of them with themes.  You have a remarkable creative mind and a blazing work ethic.  You have entertained me often, including today.  Thank you sir!

I often find myself in this situation: I am in awe of the setter for their amazing idea and the brilliant execution, but still disgruntled about a lot of the unguessable crosses — MILO/ILDIVO being a case in point. 

The problem is that when you have an error in the filled grid, you can fiddle endlessly with the known unknowns, but you can’t be sure that your fiddling is going to complete the whole puzzle, because there might be unknown errors lurking elsewhere. So it doesn’t help to know you’ve got one bit wrong, and you end up having to check. (ie cheat) 

So my overall feeling is slight dissatisfaction and disgruntlement, while knowing that i am just being a curmudgeon in the face of genius.

In case you're wondering why the 110A film TWELVEANGRYMEN featured an all-male jury, here is some interesting information from the internet:

[In 1957, state jury qualifications varied widely. Three states (Alabama, South Carolina, and Mississippi) completely barred women from serving by law, while many other states used "opt-in" systems or automatic exemptions for homemakers that kept female participation extremely low.]

[The Civil Rights Act of 1957 first made women eligible to serve on federal juries across all states regardless of local state laws, but actual representation remained minimal.]

[Low participation rates are famously reflected in the 1957 film 12 Angry Men, which featured an all-male jury—a scenario that was entirely normal and accurate for courtrooms of that era. It was not until the Jury Selection and Service Act of 1968 and later 1975 Supreme Court rulings that systemic sex discrimination in juries was prohibited nationwide.]

I notice that there is, as of this writing, no comment from my comrade-in-arms, Andrjez, who usually agrees with me regarding John Kugelman's puzzles. I think I know the reason.

I print out the puzzle. I don't have a color printer. Sunday's puzzles are always in tiny print, due to the size. and I have a vision problem. The absence of color made those rebuses pretty much unreadable. On my page, the lighthouse seemed to be shining on a pumpkin. I couldn't tell what those critters were. The lion was doing something, but what? What made those boys bad, a mere skull on their shirts? The only one that was a slam dunk for me was TWELVE ANGRY MEN IN BLACK, and I had to squint to count them to verify that my instinct was correct, but I couldn't see the expression on their faces. 

Nevertheless, the puzzle was easy enough that I was able to figure out all the answers without having to look up anything, even without being a film devotee. Long answers are usually easier to get than short ones. But nothing in this puzzle made me change my mind about puzzles by John Kugelman. I know I'm certainly in the minority, but I wish the editors would end their love affair with his puzzles.

Good heavens. I thought this was just fine, and the illustrations were cute—I solve on a laptop, because a phone makes everything too small. It's a practice I heartily recommend for my fellow glasses-wearers. 

But as for the moaning about contemporary slang and references (and many are hardly contemporary): certainly few are obscure, at least to me (for instance,FUNfetti can be well known to anyone who strolls the grocery aisle, and FURSONAS has been around for a while). Others, like IOMMI, are outside of my wheelhouse but that doesn't make them obscure in general. Besides, they're mostly gettable on the crosses and clearly in someone else's Goldilocks zone. 

If you want to see obscure, try the first crossword ever published by the NYT, in 1942. I've hacked away at it periodically for over two years, and I'm nowhere near complete. But that's on me, not on the constructor.

@Lewis, I've been looking into the "please" question and noticed a couple of things: first, that English used to be like Danish. The use of "please" to make a polite request is relatively modern, having been trimmed down from phrases such as "if it pleases you". (The phrase uses "please" in the sense of "to bring pleasure or satisfaction", which Danish does have words for!)

Second, several Romance languages don't seem to have a word for "please", either. For example, Spanish uses the phrase "por favor", meaning "as a favor"; Portuguese and Italian are similar. French has "s'il vous plait", which means "if it pleases you".

@Bob the difference between the romance languages and Danish is that "por favor" and "s'il vous plaît" can each be translated as a unit to the word "please". There is no word or phrase in Danish that would translate as "please". The closest is "venligst", kindly, as in "vent venligst" - kindly wait. But there isn't a set combination of words that mean please in a vacuum. If Danes want to say "please" on its own ("but pleeease, Mom"), they use the English word "please".
